newsitem.title: USA: GM Canada strike could cost up to $150 mln a week.
newsitem.headline: GM Canada strike could cost up to $150 mln a week.

text.p: An autoworker strike at all of General Motors Corp's Canadian operations could cost the automaker up to $150 million a week in lost profits and squeeze vehicle inventories in as little as one week, analysts said.

Canadian Auto Worker members negotiating a new labor pact are poised to walk off the job at midnight on Wednesday at three GM assembly operations in Canada, including a truck facility in Oshawa, Ontario that makes two-thirds of the company's extended cab C/K full-size pickups for North America.

GM could lose between $50 million and $60 million a week from the shutdown of the assembly operations alone, said David Healy, analyst at Burnham Securities Inc. A full-fledged shutdown could take $150 million a week out of profits, he said.

If the strike spreads later in the week to a Windsor, Ontario transmission plant as threatened, it could hurt the production launch of the new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass cars, said Mike Robinet, managing director of CSM Forecasting in Farmington Hills, Mich.
The plant is the sole supplier of four-speed, electronic automatic transmissions for the two new cars, which are scheduled to begin production in two weeks.
It also makes transmissions for the Chevrolet Cavalier and Pontiac Sunfire, as well as the Oldsmobile Achieva, Pontiac Grand Am and Buick Skylark.
But it is on the popular C/K pickups that GM would most quickly feel the heat. The Oshawa truck plant is the only one in North America that produces C/K pickups with the optional third-door.
"In a matter of a week or so, you'll find delivery being pushed back," Robinet said.

Inventory numbers for September are not yet available. But at the end of August, there was a 64-day supply of all C/K models on dealer lots, according to Ward's Automotive Reports, an industry trade publication.
Analysts cautioned, however, that the supply for the hot-selling extended cabs and three-doors is probably below that. The industry generally considers a 60-day supply to be ideal.

A work stoppage at the Canadian parts plants would also crimp sales of GM's full-size sport/utilities. GM's St. Catherines, Ontario, component facility makes axles for the Chevrolet Tahoe and GMC Yukon and Suburban sport/utilities.

Other assembly plants that would be hit by a strike on Wednesday are a car operation in Oshawa that makes the Lumina, Monte Carlo, Regal and Century; and the Ste. Therese plant in Quebec that makes the Camaro and Firebird. All of those cars have healthy inventory levels.

Although it contains some important parts plants, Healy noted GM's Canadian operations would not bring the automaker to its knees, like the 17-day work stoppage at two Dayton, Ohio, brake plants in March did. GM has a total of 20 locations in Canada, where about 26,000 CAW members work.
The strike potential has captured the attention of dealers, who have been battling tight supplies of full-size pickups for months.

"Any type of a truck strike that could stop any of the production is a concern," said Steve Kash, general sales manager of Bill Heard Chevrolet in Columbus, Ga. "It's difficult to retail it if you don't have it."
